transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Polaris), Markus Vogel (Polaris SRE), Priya Nair (Polaris Head of ML), Samir Desai (Polaris Infra), Aisha Bello (Polaris Security)

Auto-summary: Focus was on practical steps to get token-level traces into Polaris's existing OTEL/Jaeger/Prom stack, how to interpret KV cache hits/misses in traces, and how batching/quantization choices affect end-to-end tail latency and cost. Action items were assigned.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? We, uh, sent a short agenda — Ravi is going to run through the runtime tracing bits and then we'll workshop what you need on your side.
[00:18] Lena (Polaris): Hi — Lena here, platform eng. We're especially interested in token-level visibility so we can correlate latency spikes to cache behavior.
[00:28] Markus (Polaris SRE): Markus — we run Prom/Jaeger and want to avoid adding too much cardinality to Prom.
[00:34] Priya (ML): Priya — curious about quantization effects on output quality when you route to quantized variants during high load.
[00:42] Ravi (Redwood SE): Great. I'll share my screen, show an OTLP exporter example and how traces look when a KV cache hit short-circuits decoding.

[02:10] Ravi: OK real quick — Redwood Runtime emits a span per request plus per-token child spans if you enable per-token tracing. Each token span includes token_index, token_text (optional), kv_cache_hit boolean, batch_size, and selected kernel path. The exporter supports OTLP over gRPC and also a light-weight UDP aggregator we call the span-forwarder.
[02:42] Samir (Polaris Infra): Wait — token_text optional? we can't send full tokens to our vendor. Need to PII filter — are there fields you can drop?
[02:49] Ravi: Yes, token_text is optional. You can drop or hash the token and keep only token_id. We also support tag filtering at export time.
[03:15] Aisha (Security): We'll need the KMS-backed signing and transfer over private link. Anything that goes out of the VPC needs to be approved.
[03:22] Maya: Noted — we support OTLP over a VPC peering / private link; for on-prem we can run the console agent inside your VPC and send only metrics to Redwood.

[04:05] [Screen share noise, Ravi narrating]
[04:22] Ravi: Here's a sample trace from a 512-token prompt. Notice the prefix caching: you see an early KV cache hit on token 0-64 which reduces decoding spans later. There's a spike at token 187 where batching forced a late kernel selection — you'll see that reflected in the kernel_path tag.
[05:05] Markus: That kernel_path tag — can we map to hardware? Like cuda kernel v1 vs v2, or CPU fallback?
[05:12] Ravi: Yes, kernel_path maps to the execution path; we annotate it with hardware and quantization level, e.g., gpu_80_q4 or cpu_f32. That helps you filter perf regressions per kernel.

[06:00] Lena: How does batching affect the token spans? If we batch 8 vs 32, do we still get per-token timing or do token spans merge?
[06:12] Ravi: Good question. We emit logical per-token spans, but wall-clock timestamps will reflect batching—if a batch delayed decoding by 30ms, you'll see that in token-level duration. There's also a batch_id attribute so you can aggregate. We recommend sampling at batch-level for steady-state, and higher sampling for errors or tails.
[07:00] Priya: Sampling — happy to reduce volume, but we need enough samples in tail latencies to correlate with quality regressions. Any suggestions?
[07:10] Ravi: Common pattern: keep deterministic sampling for 1% of all requests, and triggered full tracing when latency > SLO or when output evals drop. We also support tag-based triggers (model mismatch, quantization fallback).

[08:20] [Brief crosstalk — someone types in chat a link to an internal dashboard]
[08:45] Markus: We're concerned about Prom's cardinality — creating a metric per token_index will blow up. How do others do this?
[08:52] Maya: You avoid high-card metrics. We push token-level as traces not metrics; aggregate metrics at route/model/batch_size/KV_cache_hit buckets. For Prom you get summary counters like token_latency_p50/p95 with labels for kv_hit:true/false, quant_level.
[09:30] Aisha: And for compliance, how long do traces persist? We need 90 days of audit logs.
[09:36] Ravi: Redwood Console can retain trace metadata for configurable retention; full trace payloads we can keep per customer policy — i.e., 30/90/365 days. For on-prem deployments you control retention fully.

[11:00] [Ravi shows flamegraph from trace viewer]
[11:25] Ravi: This flamegraph shows hotspots — decoding vs KV lookup vs dispatch. You'll often see KV cache miss causing a big spike in lookup time. The KV cache hit path is usually <5ms, miss can be 30-120ms depending on model size and disk tier.
[12:02] Lena: Disk tier — are we talking SSD vs NVMe vs remote object store?
[12:10] Ravi: Exactly. On-prem you can pin KV cache to local NVMe for fastest hits; Redwood Dedicated uses local instance storage or NVMe-backed nodes. When KV is backed by S3-like object storage misses will be much worse.

[13:00] Markus: How about quantization — do you annotate spans when you route to a quantized variant?
[13:08] Ravi: Yes model_variant and quant_level are tags on spans. You can filter traces where quant_level=q5 or q8. We also emit a quality_score estimate from the eval harness when enabled.
[13:35] Priya: Quality score estimate — that's interesting. How reliable is it?
[13:42] Ravi: It’s an approximate heuristic — embedding-similarity to golden responses plus a few rule-based checks. Not perfect but helpful for flagging regressions.

[15:00] Lena: On instrumentation — what's the perf overhead of enabling token spans?
[15:10] Ravi: Per-token spans add CPU and network overhead. In our tests per-token tracing at full sample rate increased latency by ~6-12% and token emission rate dropped modestly. That's why we recommend low sampling or triggered tracing on anomalies.
[15:35] Markus: So if we enable per-token full tracing in staging for 48 hours and run a soak test, we'll catch most of the kernel regressions?
[15:44] Ravi: Yep, that's a good plan. Also include representative batch-size distributions and prompt lengths.

[17:00] [Screen: OTLP collector config]
[17:15] Ravi: Here's an example collector config to ingest OTLP spans and forward to Jaeger and a long-term trace store. Note that for privacy you can strip token_text and only export token_id. We also support a transform to sample-by-batch and drop certain high-card tags before export.
[18:02] Samir: Does your exporter support gzip or protobuf compression? Bandwidth matters.
[18:08] Ravi: Yes OTLP/gRPC with gzip compression is supported. Also batching the exporter improves throughput but adds a few ms of exporter latency.

[19:00] Aisha: From a security standpoint, we need SAML SSO for the Console, RBAC for team-level access, and HSM-backed keys for any keys leaving our VPC.
[19:10] Maya: Redwood Console supports SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. For private deployments keys never leave your environment unless you opt in. We'll send the SOC 2 + deployment checklist.

[20:40] Priya: One more thing — if we do quantization fallback under high load (i.e., route to q4 model), will the traces indicate that the response came from fallback?
[20:51] Ravi: Yes there’s an explicit fallback_reason tag and original_model requested. We also emit latency delta between primary and fallback so you can understand perf cost and quality delta.

[22:10] [Discussion of dashboards]
[22:25] Maya: Suggested dashboard tiles: token latency p50/p95 split by kv_hit true/false, per-kernel failure rate, quantization fallback rate, and a trace sample viewer for tail traces. We can share Grafana templates.
[22:42] Markus: We use Grafana + Loki + Jaeger. Will the Redwood OTLP collector play nicely with our Loki logs?
[22:50] Ravi: Yes — you can correlate traces with logs via trace_id injection into logs, or send KV cache metrics to Prom and logs to Loki; Redwood's trace_id is compatible with OpenTelemetry trace id, so linking is straightforward.

[24:00] Lena: Any gotchas for on-prem?
[24:06] Ravi: On-prem you need to size NVMe for KV cache, and ensure enough NIC bandwidth for exporters if you do high sampling. Also ensure kernel module compatibility for CUDA / MIG isolation if running mixed workloads.
[24:45] Samir: Our firewall rules will require static egress ports — is the exporter port configurable?
[24:50] Maya: Yes you can pick exporter ports and use a reverse-proxy inside the VPC. We typically run the collector in-cluster and egress through a controlled gateway.

[26:00] [Short pause — someone drops in link to an internal RFC]
[26:20] Priya: Let's talk numbers — what throughput hit do you see with quantized models vs fp16?
[26:28] Ravi: In our benchmarks q4_0 can be 1.6–2.3x tokens/sec vs fp16 on the same GPU due to reduced memory bandwidth; but quality can drop slightly depending on model. We profile and provide quality-vs-cost curves per model.
[27:02] Lena: If we run a dedicated 3-node cluster, what's a ballpark for sustained 10k token/sec?
[27:10] Maya: Depends on model; for an open 13B quant model, roughly 3 A100-like GPUs could sustain bursts but throughput depends on batching. We'll send a sizing estimate with assumptions.

[28:30] Markus: Regarding alerts — what should we alert on?
[28:36] Ravi: Key alerts: sudden spike in kv_miss_rate, kernel_error_rate, quant_fallback_rate, and a divergence between model_quality_score and baseline. Also backward-in-time increases in p99 token latency.

[30:00] [Deep-dive: tracing example broken down]
[30:12] Ravi: Walkthrough: request span -> tokenizer -> kv-lookup spans tagged with cache_key and hit boolean -> model forward pass split by microkernels -> decode spans for each token. If you hook into the trace viewer you can zoom into the token where a quality check fails and see whether a cache miss or kernel fallback happened.
[31:05] Lena: Could we instrument our own internal pre- and post-processing to pass custom attributes into spans?
[31:12] Ravi: Yes you can pass customer_tags with a max cardinality constraint. We recommend low-card tags like route and customer_env, not user_id.

[32:40] Priya: Bench question — how do you validate that a perf regression is due to a kernel change vs bad prompts?
[32:48] Ravi: Correlate kernel_path changes with tail traces across many requests. If kernel_path is stable but latency increases, look at batch patterns and KV_miss_rate. If kernel_path changed right before spike, it's likely a kernel update. We also recommend canary rollouts with trace sampling enabled.

[34:00] [Customer asks about cost model]
[34:12] Maya: Cost levers: batching (higher batch => lower tokens/unit cost but higher tail latency), cache hit rate (higher hit => lower per-token GPU time), quantization (lower precision => lower memory & faster kernels), and model routing (smaller models for simple prompts).
[35:00] Markus: For billing, can we get token-level chargeback?
[35:06] Maya: Yes Redwood Console provides token-level cost attribution per API key and route. We can also export cost metrics to your billing system.

[36:20] [There is a short interruption: someone on the call drops and rejoins]
[37:05] Priya: For the pilot we want to run: 48 hours of per-token traces in staging with 1% steady sample + full traces on SLO breaches. We'll send sample prompts and expected traffic shape.
[37:18] Maya: Sounds good. We'll provide the collector config and sample dashboards, and Ravi will prepare the export helm chart.

[38:40] [Security corner — Aisha asks about key handling]
[38:52] Aisha: How do you manage trace export credentials? We don't want long-lived secrets in the cluster.
[39:00] Ravi: Use short-lived tokens via STS or mTLS with cert rotation. On-prem we can use instance identity or inject via your vault. We'll include examples.

[41:00] Lena: Let's role-play an incident: a user reports hallucinations on a produced story. How do we triage?
[41:12] Ravi: Triage steps: 1) pull tail traces for the request id; 2) check kv_hit flag around problematic tokens; 3) check quant_fallback or kernel_fallback; 4) check model_version and recent rollouts; 5) run eval harness on the prompt set to see if quality regressed. Traces give you the timeline to see if the problem is model, routing, or cache.

[44:00] [Discussion of integration timeline]
[44:20] Maya: Proposed timeline: day 1 share collector config and dashboard templates; day 3 ingest first trace samples; day 7 run 48hr soak in staging; by week 3 review pilot results and sizing.
[45:10] Markus: Need approval from infra for peering — I'll schedule that this week.

[47:00] [Ravi shows an example alert rule and a Grafana dashboard JSON snippet]
[47:30] Ravi: The dashboard includes p95 token latency by kv_hit, kernel_path heatmap, and a top-100 slow traces table.
[48:10] Priya: Can we do automated regression alerts based on the quality_score?
[48:18] Ravi: Yes — we have webhooks from the eval system that can post to Slack/pager when quality drops beyond a threshold.

[50:00] Aisha: Last compliance note — for on-prem, we need audit logs of who accessed traces. Is that supported?
[50:08] Maya: Yes Console audit logs include user, IP, timestamp, and trace ids viewed. For private deployments logs stay in your account.

[52:00] [Recap and next steps]
[52:10] Maya: Quick recap — deliverables: OTLP collector config, Grafana templates, SOC2 + on-prem checklist, pricing and sizing estimate, and pilot contract draft. Ravi will produce exporter helm chart.
[52:30] Lena: We'll provide representative prompts and traffic profile, and coordinate on peering windows.
[52:40] Maya: Great. Any final questions?
[52:44] Markus: One: can we get a sample of the trace retention UI?
[52:48] Maya: We'll include screenshots in the packet.
[53:00] Priya: Also please include the model quality vs quantization curves for the 13B family.
[53:08] Ravi: Will do.

[56:00] [Minor tangential discussion about internal benchmark naming conventions — minor laughter]
[57:05] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot kick-off.
[57:20] Lena: Thanks — looking forward.
[57:30] [Call ends around 17:32 UTC — someone leaves a link to a GitHub repo in chat]

Notes about transcript quality: occasional speaker mislabels ("Speaker 2" present), minor ASR errors in technical names (e.g., "kernel path" typed as "kernel-path"), some filler words left in.

End of transcript.
